fact.en: Trap: Confusing the initiator of the Tripartite Struggle. The struggle for Kannauj was initiated by Vatsaraja, NOT Nagabhata I. Nagabhata I successfully fought the Arabs but did not start the Tripartite Struggle.
fact.hi: Trap: Confusing the initiator of the Tripartite Struggle. The struggle for Kannauj was initiated by Vatsaraja, NOT Nagabhata I. Nagabhata I successfully fought the Arabs but did not start the Tripartite Struggle.

fact.en: Trap: Believing the Gurjara-Pratiharas were defeated by the Palas permanently. Vatsaraja defeated Dharmapala (Pala king), and later Nagabhata II also defeated Dharmapala at Mudgagiri. The main threat that pushed back the Pratiharas was the Deccan-based Rashtrakutas.
fact.hi: Trap: Believing the Gurjara-Pratiharas were defeated by the Palas permanently. Vatsaraja defeated Dharmapala (Pala king), and later Nagabhata II also defeated Dharmapala at Mudgagiri. The main threat that pushed back the Pratiharas was the Deccan-based Rashtrakutas.

fact.en: Trap: Assuming Rajashekhara wrote exclusively in Sanskrit. Although he wrote major treatises like Kavyamimansa in Sanskrit, his highly acclaimed play Karpuramanjari was written entirely in Sauraseni Prakrit.

fact.en: Trap: Confusing the reigns under which Arab travelers visited. Sulaiman visited during the reign of Mihira Bhoja (Bhoja I) in the 9th century, whereas Al-Masudi visited during the reign of Mahipala I (early 10th century).

fact.en: Trap: Believing the Gurjara-Pratiharas were an Agnikula clan according to all historical sources. The Agnikula origin (born from fire at Mt. Abu) is a legend popularized by the late medieval text Prithviraj Raso by Chand Bardai. Early epigraphic records like the Gwalior Prasasti describe them as descendants of Lakshmana (brother of Rama), who acted as a 'Pratihara' (doorkeeper).
